nameStory: The name 'grandaeva' comes from Latin meaning 'of great age' or 'ancient,' suggesting this spider represents a very old evolutionary lineage. The genus name Estrandia honors the scientists who first studied these tiny, ancient spiders. With only one known species in the entire genus, this spider is like finding a living fossil in the web world!
description: Estrandia grandaeva is an extremely rare dwarf spider, so tiny you'd need a magnifying glass to see its details clearly. Like other dwarf spiders in the sheetweb family, it's likely smaller than a pencil eraser and builds delicate sheet webs close to the ground. This spider is incredibly uncommon in New England - so rare that it's been recorded only once in our region! Its small size and secretive nature make it one of the most elusive spiders you might never actually encounter.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny, likely measuring just 2-3 millimeters long - about the size of a grain of rice or smaller

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds delicate sheet webs close to the ground, feeling papery-thin and almost invisible until dewdrops reveal them

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Typical dwarf spider proportions with a rounded abdomen and relatively long, thin legs for its tiny body size

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely secretive and stays hidden in leaf litter or low vegetation - you'll need to search very carefully in moist, sheltered spots

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England, the specific habitat preferences here are unclear, but it likely favors moist, sheltered areas with dense leaf litter or low vegetation. Look in undisturbed forest floors, particularly in areas with rich organic matter and consistent moisture. The single New England record suggests it may prefer cooler, more northern forest types.

seasonality.spring: Most likely active period as temperatures warm and prey becomes abundant. Adult specimens would be easiest to spot during this season if present.
seasonality.summer: May remain active but becomes even more secretive during hot, dry periods. Look for tiny sheet webs in the coolest, most humid microclimates.
seasonality.fall: Activity likely decreases as the spider prepares for winter. Any remaining webs become more fragile and harder to detect.
seasonality.winter: Probably overwinters in a protected stage, either as eggs or immature spiders deep in leaf litter or soil crevices.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that you're more likely to discover a new species than find this one - it's been recorded exactly once in our entire region, making it like the unicorn of New England spiders!
confusionNotes: With only one sighting in New England, it's nearly impossible to distinguish from other tiny dwarf spiders without expert examination under a microscope. If you find any extremely small spider with a sheet web, it's far more likely to be one of the common dwarf spider species.
contextualKnowledge: This spider represents a fascinating biogeographical puzzle - primarily known from Asia (China, Japan, Russia), its presence in New England raises questions about how it arrived here and whether it represents a relict population or recent introduction.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus, Estrandia grandaeva stands alone evolutionarily. Compared to other dwarf spiders in the Linyphiidae family found in New England, it's distinguished mainly by its extreme rarity and its unique genetic lineage. Without microscopic examination of reproductive structures, it's virtually impossible to separate from other tiny sheet-web builders in the field.
